name: Tomas Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. This is confidential. Tell me what an ordinary day at the contact centre is like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43, a junior agent on calls and chats, and still learning the tricky returns. I finished secondary school and earn at the low end of the centre. I use AI every day to draft a reply and find the right policy, but I still get slow when a customer has more than one account.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Elin, and I have two school-age children and a mortgage. She works shifts at a grocery shop; we have less than a month of expenses saved, and there are few other centres nearby. I like testing a tool before the morning queue fills up. I also like having dinner with my family without a headset in my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AI Plateau is about a faster first draft, like the tool I already use. I would still open the return rule myself before promising a customer money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my work remains, but a quiet AI year does not make our mortgage easier. One short grocery-shop week for Elin could use up what little we saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking calls and checking the daily draft against the policy page. In the first year of this small change, I’d put the money from two weekly snack purchases into an account for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the next bill, though calm about the tool. A quicker draft cannot pay the house if my partner Elin’s rota drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which expense could you shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would give the children fruit from home after school instead of buying a snack on the way back. They can still have a treat sometimes, but the saved amount goes into the house account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error did your tool make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week a draft said an opened item could go back for a full refund. I checked the rule and corrected it before the customer left with a promise we could not keep.

say: I’d call AI a **first draft** that still needs a policy check.
I’d tell colleagues a wrong **refund promise** harms customers.
think: I think my **work remains** under a small change.
I worry Elin’s **shop shifts** could still break our budget.
do: Keep **taking calls** and verifying AI drafts in 2026.
Save **snack money** for the mortgage during the first year.
feel: **Anxious** about bills, calmer about the tool.
S0.quote: A quicker draft cannot pay the house if my partner Elin’s rota drops.
fieldNote: His **mortgage worry** predates any large AI change.
He caught a **refund error** before sending a false promise.
A modest **snack cut** reflects the family’s thin reserve.

steps.text: Keep taking calls and checking drafted replies against return policy
Save the cost of two weekly after-school snacks for the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will take many standard chats, and we should find out which human cases are still paid work. I’d ask the supervisor to show the new answer tool on real returns, not a polished demo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my simple chats may disappear before I am fast on difficult disputes. Elin’s shop wage will not cover the mortgage if my hours fall, and there are few other centres nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d take a paid practice shift on difficult returns if one is offered and test the new answer tool against actual policy pages. In the first year routine chats move, I’d apply for a posted customer desk role with mortgage-covering hours and cut the family’s paid video plan if my roster shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, with a bit of energy to learn. I can click a tool quickly, but I cannot learn a whole job on unpaid evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you practise the harder cases?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask an experienced agent to sit with me on three difficult returns during a paid shift. I would write down where the answer tool missed an exception, then try the same check myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cost would fall first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Elin (my partner) we should cancel the paid video plan before touching school food. We can borrow films from friends, but not a mortgage payment.

say: I’d ask for **real return tests** before changing the queue.
I’d say **standard chats** may leave junior agents with harder calls.
think: I think my **simple chats** could vanish before I master disputes.
I know Elin’s **shop wage** cannot cover the mortgage alone.
do: Take **paid return practice** and test the new answer tool in 2026 if offered.
Seek a **posted desk job** and cut video fees if hours fall in the first year.
S1.quote: I can click a tool quickly, but I cannot learn a whole job on unpaid evenings.
fieldNote: He wants **paid practice** with actual return exceptions.
Daily **AI use** does not erase his junior standing.
The family would cut **video fees** before school food.

steps.text: Take a paid difficult-return practice shift with an experienced agent if offered
Test the new answer tool against three actual return policies
Apply for a posted customer desk role with mortgage-covering hours if shifts fall
Cancel the family video plan if his roster shrinks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 could answer every chat I am still learning to handle. I’d ask for a written list of paid vacancies before any rota is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think a cheap thinking system could take my whole headset day in 2028. Robots arrive around 2031, but I do not lift parcels at work; we have less than a month saved for mortgage and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d stop looking at a replacement car and put any extra shop or centre pay into the house account. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid service desk role only if its hours cover the mortgage, and ask Elin’s parents for one bill’s help only if both wages dip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and the short clock makes my stomach go tight. A clever screen cannot fill the gap between a payday and the mortgage date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say about the car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Elin (my partner) the car can keep running if it is safe. A new loan would use money we might need for the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would family be able to bridge the gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Elin’s parents might help for one month, but they have their own costs. I would ask them only after we have looked at paid openings and know exactly which bill is short.

say: I’d ask management for **paid vacancy lists** before any 2028 shift cuts arrive.
I’d tell colleagues **2028 thinking AI** matters before robots.
think: I think AGI could take my **whole headset day**.
I fear **mortgage arrears** with less than a month saved.
do: Defer a **car loan** only while the current car is safe, and save extra pay in 2026.
Apply for **posted paid service work** after 2028 only if its hours cover the mortgage.
Ask Elin’s **parents** about one bill only if both wages dip, after checking openings and the shortfall.
feel: **Alarmed** by the short runway and fragile bills.
S2.quote: A clever screen cannot fill the gap between a payday and the mortgage date.
fieldNote: He correctly focuses on the **2028 thinking-work date**.
He delays a **car loan** to keep household cash available.
Family support is a **one-bill bridge**, not ongoing income.

steps.text: Delay replacing the car only while safe to drive, avoiding a new loan
Put extra shift pay into the mortgage account from 2026
Apply for posted paid service work with mortgage-covering hours after 2028
Ask Elin’s parents about one bill only if both wages dip, after checking openings and shortfall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives time to find out whether a new role exists before we train for it. I would ask for the wage beside every course name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years might let me learn enough difficult cases for a service desk, but a desk could face the same thinking AI. I cannot spend our mortgage buffer on a certificate with no posted work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d ask for a paid difficult-case shift each month and take it if the centre offers one. In the first year after 2031, I’d apply for a posted service role with mortgage-covering hours and take an employer-funded course only if it is required for that named opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years gives me time to see whether practice turns into wages. I cannot feed the children with a course title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that shift teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the senior agent to show me why three returned items were handled differently. I would practise checking the account and policy side by side on paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a course worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Elin (my partner) the course must be funded by an employer hiring for an actual role. Otherwise I would keep our money for the mortgage and search the few centres nearby.

say: I’d ask employers to put **wages beside courses** before we spend time studying.
I’d say five years lets us **test roles** before training.
think: I think I could learn **difficult cases** over five years.
I doubt another **screen desk** is safe forever.
do: Take **monthly paid case practice** if offered from 2026.
Apply for **posted service work** after 2031; take only required employer-funded training.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to test real work.
S3.quote: I cannot spend our mortgage buffer on a certificate with no posted work.
fieldNote: His **paid practice** protects evenings with the family.
A course requires an **employer-funded named opening**.
He keeps the **mortgage buffer** out of speculative training.
He would search the **few nearby centres** while keeping his current wage.

steps.text: Take employer-funded training only if required for a named posted service vacancy
Apply for a posted service role with mortgage-covering hours after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives my children time to see grown-ups learn new work without panic. I would still ask the centre for paid shifts on the harder cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could be more useful by 53, but full thinking AI may still take phone work. Robots around 2039 are later, and the mortgage is due now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep the call job, take a paid difficult-case shift monthly if offered and save part of each pay. In the first year after 2036, I’d apply for posted service work only where the wage and hours cover the mortgage; I would keep the children in their school unless a signed offer justified moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about present bills, less rushed about 2036. Ten years gives me time to practise, not ten years without a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn one exception at a time with a senior agent on the paid rota. I might be quick with tools, but I need the person beside me to explain why a customer’s story matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the family move for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not uproot the children for a possible opening. Elin (my partner) and I would need a signed wage and a school route we can manage before moving.

say: I’d ask for **paid hard-case shifts** over the decade.
I’d tell children adults can **learn new work** without panic.
think: I think I could become **more useful** by 53.
I know **2036 thinking AI** may still take my calls.
do: Keep **calling**, practise monthly if paid and save each pay.
Seek **posted service work** after 2036 at mortgage-covering wages.
feel: **Anxious** about bills, less rushed by the longer horizon.
S4.quote: Ten years gives me time to practise, not ten years without a mortgage.
fieldNote: Current **mortgage pressure** keeps his mood anxious.
He values **apprentice-style learning** beside an experienced agent.
He protects the **children’s school** unless a signed offer makes moving safe.

steps.text: Keep taking call shifts while they pay the mortgage
Take a monthly paid difficult-case shift if offered
Save a small part of each pay for the mortgage
Apply for posted service work with mortgage-covering wage and hours after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 frightens me most. It could take the simple calls that make up most of my shift before I have learned the hard cases, and our mortgage has no two-year pause. I would need a posted paid role with enough hours for the house and paid training tied to that real vacancy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I wish you had asked about first jobs. My children will need someone to let them try a task beside an experienced worker, even if a machine is faster.

headlineQuote: My children will need someone to let them try a task beside an experienced worker, even if a machine is faster.
portrait: At **43**, Tomas is a junior call agent still learning difficult returns after secondary school.
He and Elin support **two children** and a mortgage on low pay with less than one month saved.
He uses **AI daily** and tests tools early, though multiple-account calls still slow him.
He wants **paid openings** and practical learning tied to work that covers the mortgage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his simple calls before he has learned harder work or built savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **posted paid job** with mortgage-covering hours and paid training tied to it would help.
